GARMENT MANUFACTURING REGISTRATION AND BRAND GUARANTOR WAGE LIABILITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Apparel, Inc.

ABOUT THIS GARMENT MANUFACTURING REGISTRATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's garment manufacturing statutes, Labor Code Part 11 of Division 2 (Sections 2670 through 2693.1), which require every person engaged in the business of garment manufacturing to register with the Labor Commissioner, impose recordkeeping and hourly-pay rules on that industry, and make garment manufacturers, contractors, and "brand guarantors" jointly and severally liable for the unpaid wages of the workers who make their garments. Acme Apparel, Inc. has described its garment manufacturing or garment contracting activity, if any, as follows: We design apparel under our own label and contract with two Los Angeles sewing shops. This document states the content of the statutes and of one published California appellate decision construing them; it does not determine whether any particular business, product line, or contracting arrangement falls within the statutory definitions, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

WHO THE GARMENT MANUFACTURING STATUTES COVER: "GARMENT MANUFACTURING," "CONTRACTOR," AND "BRAND GUARANTOR"
Labor Code Section 2671 supplies the definitions used throughout Part 11. "Garment manufacturing" is defined expansively to include sewing, cutting, making, processing, repairing, finishing, assembling, dyeing, altering a garment's design, causing another person to alter a garment's design, affixing a label to a garment, or otherwise preparing any garment or article of wearing apparel or accessories intended to be worn, including clothing, hats, gloves, handbags, hosiery, ties, scarfs, and belts, for sale or resale. A "garment manufacturer" is any person engaged in garment manufacturing who is not a contractor; a "contractor" is a person who, with the assistance of employees or others, is engaged in garment manufacturing by primarily performing those operations for another person, and includes a subcontractor primarily engaged in those operations. A "brand guarantor" is any person contracting for the performance of garment manufacturing, whether or not the person it contracts with performs the operations itself or hires contractors or subcontractors to do so, and the statute states that contracts for the performance of garment manufacturing include the licensing of a brand or name. Section 2671(a) also excludes from the defined term "person" anyone who manufactures garments alone without the assistance of a contractor, employee, or others, anyone engaged solely in cleaning, alteration, or tailoring, and anyone engaged in the regulated activities as an employee whose sole compensation is wages.

The statute also does not state how the "primarily engaging" qualifier in the "contractor" definition is measured.

THE REGISTRATION REQUIREMENT AND ITS CONDITIONS (LABOR CODE SECTION 2675)
Labor Code Section 2675(a) requires every person engaged in the business of garment manufacturing to register with the Labor Commissioner, and states that the Commissioner may neither permit registration nor allow renewal until each of the listed conditions is satisfied. Those conditions include a written application in the form the Commissioner prescribes, subscribed and sworn by the applicant, stating the facts the Commissioner requires about the applicant's character, competency, and responsibility and the manner and method by which the applicant proposes to engage in the business, together with the names, addresses, and interests of all persons financially interested in the proposed business other than bona fide salaried employees (a listing of principal officers suffices for a publicly traded corporation); an investigation leaving the Commissioner satisfied as to the applicant's character, competency, and responsibility; documentation that a current workers' compensation insurance policy is in effect for the applicant's employees; and payment of an initial or renewal registration fee set by the Labor Commissioner based on the applicant's annual volume, with a statutory floor of $250 and ceilings of $1,000 for contractors and $2,500 for all other registrants.

EXAMINATION, SAFETY ATTESTATION, RENEWAL, AND POSTING OF THE REGISTRATION FORM
Labor Code Section 2675(c) conditions first-time registration and renewal on demonstrating, by oral or written examination or both, knowledge of the laws and administrative regulations concerning garment manufacturing that the Labor Commissioner deems necessary for the safety and protection of garment workers, and knowledge of state occupational safety and health laws, which the statute specifies as including the Title 8 regulations on the Injury Prevention Program, Emergency Action Plan, Fire Prevention Plan, and portable fire extinguishers. The applicant must also sign a statement committing to comply with those safety regulations, to ensure employees are made aware of them and instructed in implementing the three plans, to ensure employees are instructed in the use of portable fire extinguishers, and to post the three plans prominently in the workplace. Section 2675(f) requires a person seeking renewal to take both examinations and sign the statement, but provides that once a renewal has been granted on that basis, further examinations are required only at the Commissioner's discretion and only if the registrant was found in the preceding year to have violated subdivision (a) or a section enumerated in it. Section 2675(g) provides that proof of registration is an official Division of Labor Standards Enforcement registration form, which must be posted where employees can read it during the workday.

WHEN A BOND IS A CONDITION OF REGISTRATION OR OF CONTINUED REGISTRATION
Labor Code Section 2675(a)(3) makes a surety bond a condition of registration for a person who has been cited and penalized within the prior three years under Part 11: the bond is in the sum and form the Commissioner deems sufficient and adequate to ensure future compliance, may not exceed $5,000, is payable to the people of California, and benefits employees of the registrant damaged by a failure to pay wages and fringe benefits or by a violation of Section 2677.5. In C & C Partners, Ltd. v. Department of Industrial Relations, the Court of Appeal held that this bond requirement is mandatory for all manufacturers who have violated the statute within three years, and rejected the argument that a bond may be required only where employees have already been damaged. Separately, Labor Code Section 2679(a) authorizes the Commissioner, in addition to any civil penalty, to require as a condition of continued registration that an employer deposit a bond within 10 days to ensure payment of wages and benefits, in an amount not exceeding $10,000, or to accept other evidence of financial security in lieu of a bond; subdivision (b) makes that bond mandatory on a second or subsequent violation within any two-year period and permits revocation of registration for 30 days to one year on a third or subsequent violation within a two-year period.

CONSEQUENCES OF OPERATING WITHOUT REGISTRATION: MISDEMEANOR AND PER-EMPLOYEE CIVIL PENALTIES
Labor Code Section 2676 makes any person engaged in the business of garment manufacturing who is not registered guilty of a misdemeanor, except as provided in Section 2678(d). Section 2678(a) authorizes a civil penalty for failing to comply with the registration requirements of Part 11, for failing to comply with Section 2673 or any section enumerated in Section 2675, and for failing to comply within 15 days of any judgment due for violation of labor laws applicable to garment industry workers; the order imposing the penalty must be in writing and describe the nature of the violation with reference to the provisions alleged to have been violated. Under Section 2678(c) the penalty is $100 for each affected employee for an initial violation and $200 for each affected employee for a second or subsequent violation, and under Section 2678(d) a violator who does not employ one or more workers is instead subject to a $500 civil penalty and is not guilty of the Section 2676 misdemeanor. In C & C Partners, Ltd. v. Department of Industrial Relations, the Court of Appeal held as a matter of first impression that when a garment manufacturer operates without a registration certificate all of its employees are "affected" for purposes of the per-employee penalty, and it rejected the contention that a penalty may not be assessed while a registration application is pending.

CONTRACTING WITH AN UNREGISTERED OR UNBONDED GARMENT BUSINESS (LABOR CODE SECTION 2677)
Labor Code Section 2677(a) provides that a person engaged in the business of garment manufacturing who contracts with another person similarly engaged who has not registered with the Commissioner, or who does not have a valid bond on file as Section 2675 requires, is deemed an employer and is jointly liable with that other person for any violation of Section 2675 and of the sections enumerated in it. Subdivision (b) permits an employee of an unregistered garment manufacturing business to bring a civil action against a person deemed an employer under subdivision (a) to recover wages, damages, or penalties owed because of the unregistered person's violation of any provision specified in Section 2675(a), or instead to file a claim with the Labor Commissioner under Section 2673.1, and it directs the court to award a prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Labor Code Section 2677.5 separately makes it illegal for a registrant contracting with another registrant to engage in any business practice that causes or is likely to cause a violation of the chapter.

JOINT AND SEVERAL WAGE LIABILITY OF MANUFACTURERS, CONTRACTORS, AND BRAND GUARANTORS (LABOR CODE SECTION 2673.1)
Labor Code Section 2673.1(a)(1) makes a garment manufacturer, contractor, or brand guarantor that contracts with another person for the performance of garment manufacturing operations jointly and severally liable with any manufacturer and contractor performing those operations for the full amount of unpaid minimum, regular, overtime, and other premium wages, reimbursement for expenses, and any other compensation including interest due to the employees who performed the operations for any violation of the Labor Code; for the employee's reasonable attorney's fees and costs under subdivision (e); and for civil penalties for failure to secure valid workers' compensation coverage as required by Section 3700. Subdivision (a)(2) preserves the parties' ability to establish, exercise, or enforce contribution and indemnity remedies against each other after a final judgment. Subdivision (b) adds that garment manufacturers and contractors are liable for the full amount of damages and penalties due to employees for a Labor Code violation, including liquidated damages equal to the wages unlawfully withheld under Section 1194.2 and liquidated damages equal to unpaid overtime compensation. Subdivision (k) provides that payment of the wages described in the section is not to be used as a basis for finding that the paying brand guarantor or registered garment manufacturer is a joint employer, coemployer, or single employer of a registered garment manufacturing contractor's employees. The Legislature stated in Section 2670(a) that this structure was intended to restore the purpose of Assembly Bill 633 (Stats. 1999, ch. 554) after manufacturers added layers of contracting to avoid guarantor liability.

THE LABOR COMMISSIONER CLAIM PROCEDURE, THE LABEL PRESUMPTION, AND APPEAL BONDS
Labor Code Section 2673.1(c) provides that employees enforce the section solely by filing a claim with the Labor Commissioner against the contractor, the garment manufacturer, and the brand guarantor, if known, and permits manufacturers and brand guarantors whose identity or existence is unknown at filing to be added later. Subdivision (d) sets mandatory deadlines: written notice and a subpoena duces tecum for books and records within 10 business days of the claim, notice to other potential manufacturers or brand guarantors within 30 days, a meet-and-confer conference within 60 days preceded by a completed investigation and assessment, a hearing commencing within 30 days and completed within 45 days of that conference, and an order, decision, or award within 15 days of the hearing's completion. Compliance with the records request within 10 days of the mailing of the notice is a condition of continued registration under Section 2675. FOUR-YEAR RECORDKEEPING DUTIES OF EMPLOYERS AND BRAND GUARANTORS (LABOR CODE SECTION 2673)
Labor Code Section 2673(a) requires every employer engaged in the business of garment manufacturing to keep accurate records for four years showing the names and addresses of all garment workers directly employed; daily hours worked including the beginning and ending times of each work period; daily production sheets including piece rates; the wages and wage rates paid each payroll period; contract worksheets indicating the price per unit agreed between contractor and manufacturer; all contracts, invoices, purchase orders, work or job orders, and style or cut sheets, including the contracting parties' business names, addresses, and contact information; a copy of the garment license of every person required to register under Section 2675 with whom the employer has contracted for garment manufacturing; the ages of all minor employees; and any other conditions of employment. PROHIBITION ON PIECE-RATE PAY FOR GARMENT MANUFACTURING WORK (LABOR CODE SECTION 2673.2)
Labor Code Section 2673.2(a) provides that an employee engaged in the performance of garment manufacturing shall not be paid by the piece or unit, or by the piece rate, and that such employees shall be paid an hourly rate not less than the applicable minimum wage. Acme Apparel, Inc. has described its garment manufacturing or garment contracting activity, if any, as follows: We design apparel under our own label and contract with two Los Angeles sewing shops. This document states the content of the statutes and of one published California appellate decision construing them; it does not determine whether any particular business, product line, or contracting arrangement falls within the statutory definitions, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

Labor Code Section 2671 supplies the definitions used throughout Part 11. "Garment manufacturing" is defined expansively to include sewing, cutting, making, processing, repairing, finishing, assembling, dyeing, altering a garment's design, causing another person to alter a garment's design, affixing a label to a garment, or otherwise preparing any garment or article of wearing apparel or accessories intended to be worn, including clothing, hats, gloves, handbags, hosiery, ties, scarfs, and belts, for sale or resale. A "garment manufacturer" is any person engaged in garment manufacturing who is not a contractor; a "contractor" is a person who, with the assistance of employees or others, is engaged in garment manufacturing by primarily performing those operations for another person, and includes a subcontractor primarily engaged in those operations. A "brand guarantor" is any person contracting for the performance of garment manufacturing, whether or not the person it contracts with performs the operations itself or hires contractors or subcontractors to do so, and the statute states that contracts for the performance of garment manufacturing include the licensing of a brand or name. Section 2671(a) also excludes from the defined term "person" anyone who manufactures garments alone without the assistance of a contractor, employee, or others, anyone engaged solely in cleaning, alteration, or tailoring, and anyone engaged in the regulated activities as an employee whose sole compensation is wages.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2676 makes any person engaged in the business of garment manufacturing who is not registered guilty of a misdemeanor, except as provided in Section 2678(d). Section 2678(a) authorizes a civil penalty for failing to comply with the registration requirements of Part 11, for failing to comply with Section 2673 or any section enumerated in Section 2675, and for failing to comply within 15 days of any judgment due for violation of labor laws applicable to garment industry workers; the order imposing the penalty must be in writing and describe the nature of the violation with reference to the provisions alleged to have been violated. Under Section 2678(c) the penalty is $100 for each affected employee for an initial violation and $200 for each affected employee for a second or subsequent violation, and under Section 2678(d) a violator who does not employ one or more workers is instead subject to a $500 civil penalty and is not guilty of the Section 2676 misdemeanor. In C & C Partners, Ltd. v. Department of Industrial Relations, the Court of Appeal held as a matter of first impression that when a garment manufacturer operates without a registration certificate all of its employees are "affected" for purposes of the per-employee penalty, and it rejected the contention that a penalty may not be assessed while a registration application is pending.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2677(a) provides that a person engaged in the business of garment manufacturing who contracts with another person similarly engaged who has not registered with the Commissioner, or who does not have a valid bond on file as Section 2675 requires, is deemed an employer and is jointly liable with that other person for any violation of Section 2675 and of the sections enumerated in it. Subdivision (b) permits an employee of an unregistered garment manufacturing business to bring a civil action against a person deemed an employer under subdivision (a) to recover wages, damages, or penalties owed because of the unregistered person's violation of any provision specified in Section 2675(a), or instead to file a claim with the Labor Commissioner under Section 2673.1, and it directs the court to award a prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Labor Code Section 2677.5 separately makes it illegal for a registrant contracting with another registrant to engage in any business practice that causes or is likely to cause a violation of the chapter.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2673.1(a)(1) makes a garment manufacturer, contractor, or brand guarantor that contracts with another person for the performance of garment manufacturing operations jointly and severally liable with any manufacturer and contractor performing those operations for the full amount of unpaid minimum, regular, overtime, and other premium wages, reimbursement for expenses, and any other compensation including interest due to the employees who performed the operations for any violation of the Labor Code; for the employee's reasonable attorney's fees and costs under subdivision (e); and for civil penalties for failure to secure valid workers' compensation coverage as required by Section 3700. Subdivision (a)(2) preserves the parties' ability to establish, exercise, or enforce contribution and indemnity remedies against each other after a final judgment. Subdivision (b) adds that garment manufacturers and contractors are liable for the full amount of damages and penalties due to employees for a Labor Code violation, including liquidated damages equal to the wages unlawfully withheld under Section 1194.2 and liquidated damages equal to unpaid overtime compensation. Subdivision (k) provides that payment of the wages described in the section is not to be used as a basis for finding that the paying brand guarantor or registered garment manufacturer is a joint employer, coemployer, or single employer of a registered garment manufacturing contractor's employees. The Legislature stated in Section 2670(a) that this structure was intended to restore the purpose of Assembly Bill 633 (Stats. 1999, ch. 554) after manufacturers added layers of contracting to avoid guarantor liability.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2673.1(c) provides that employees enforce the section solely by filing a claim with the Labor Commissioner against the contractor, the garment manufacturer, and the brand guarantor, if known, and permits manufacturers and brand guarantors whose identity or existence is unknown at filing to be added later. Subdivision (d) sets mandatory deadlines: written notice and a subpoena duces tecum for books and records within 10 business days of the claim, notice to other potential manufacturers or brand guarantors within 30 days, a meet-and-confer conference within 60 days preceded by a completed investigation and assessment, a hearing commencing within 30 days and completed within 45 days of that conference, and an order, decision, or award within 15 days of the hearing's completion. Compliance with the records request within 10 days of the mailing of the notice is a condition of continued registration under Section 2675. If the employee supplies labels or equivalent items, or other information the Commissioner finds credible identifying a brand guarantor or garment manufacturer, the statute creates a presumption that the brand guarantor or garment manufacturer is liable with the contractor, and the employee's claim of hours and amounts due is presumed valid unless rebutted by specific, compelling, and reliable written evidence including contemporaneous records. Subdivision (f) requires a contractor, garment manufacturer, or brand guarantor that appeals to post a bond equal to one and one-half times the award as a condition precedent, while no bond is required of an appealing employee.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2673(a) requires every employer engaged in the business of garment manufacturing to keep accurate records for four years showing the names and addresses of all garment workers directly employed; daily hours worked including the beginning and ending times of each work period; daily production sheets including piece rates; the wages and wage rates paid each payroll period; contract worksheets indicating the price per unit agreed between contractor and manufacturer; all contracts, invoices, purchase orders, work or job orders, and style or cut sheets, including the contracting parties' business names, addresses, and contact information; a copy of the garment license of every person required to register under Section 2675 with whom the employer has contracted for garment manufacturing; the ages of all minor employees; and any other conditions of employment. Subdivision (b) imposes a parallel four-year retention duty on brand guarantors for contract worksheets showing the agreed price per unit, the same categories of contracts and related documents, and a copy of each contracting registrant's garment license. Subdivision (c) states that these requirements are in addition to the recordkeeping requirements found elsewhere in the Labor Code, in the California Code of Regulations, and in the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2673.2(a) provides that an employee engaged in the performance of garment manufacturing shall not be paid by the piece or unit, or by the piece rate, and that such employees shall be paid an hourly rate not less than the applicable minimum wage. Subdivision (b) states that the section does not prohibit incentive-based bonuses. Subdivision (c) exempts workplaces where employees are covered by a bona fide collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours, and working conditions; premium overtime rates and a regular hourly rate at least 30 percent above the state minimum wage; stewards or monitors; and a process to resolve nonpayment disputes. Subdivisions (d) and (f) provide compensatory damages of $200 per employee for each pay period in which an employee is paid by the piece rate, recoverable through a claim filed with the Labor Commissioner against the contractor or garment manufacturer, through a Labor Commissioner action under Section 98.3, or through a citation issued under the procedures of Section 1197.1, and subdivision (g) makes statutory damages or penalties recovered under the section payable to the employee.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 2675.5(a) directs the Labor Commissioner to deposit $75 of each registrant's annual registration fee into a separate account, disbursed only to persons the Commissioner determines were damaged by a garment manufacturer's, brand guarantor's, or contractor's failure to pay wages and benefits, including interest, damages, and statutory penalties recoverable by an employee, and whether the business that owes them was registered or unregistered; recovered funds, including recovery from a surety bond, return to the account, and the remainder of each fee funds administration of Sections 2673.1, 2675, and 2675.5. Labor Code Section 2680(a) permits the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement to confiscate garments or wearing apparel assembled or partially assembled by or on behalf of a person who has not complied with the registration requirements, to hold them in custody for destruction or disposal outside the stream of commerce, and requires notice of the removal and custody location to the known manufacturer and contractor. Subdivision (b) permits the Labor Commissioner, where a contractor has had goods confiscated within the preceding five years, also to confiscate the means of production, including manufacturing equipment and the property where the unregistered operations took place, except where nonregistration resulted from delayed renewal; subdivision (c) directs sale proceeds into the Back Wages and Taxes Account in the General Fund for payment of back wages and taxes upon appropriation.
